title: Why Your Car Insurance Keeps Going Up (Even With No Accidents)
sources: Insurify, Average Car Insurance Rates (Sept 2026): national average full coverage ≈ $187/month ≈ $2,244/year; Insurify projects $2,242 full-coverage average for full-year 2026 (+1% YoY)
BLS CPI-U, Aug 2026 (released Sept 2026), series CUUR0000SETE Motor vehicle insurance: 566.183 (Aug 2021) → 848.231 (Aug 2026) = +49.8% in five years; 12-month change Aug 2026 = −5.1%
BLS CPI-U, series CUUR0000SA0 All items: 273.567 (Aug 2021) → 334.980 (Aug 2026) = +22.4% in five years
BLS CPI-U, series CUUR0000SETD Motor vehicle maintenance and repair: 320.504 (Aug 2021) → 465.136 (Aug 2026) = +45.1% in five years; +5.2% in the 12 months to Aug 2026
AAA, Cost of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) Repairs (Dec 2023): ADAS can account for up to ~38% of repair costs after a crash; front radar sensor $500–$1,300; windshield camera $900–$1,200
NHTSA, Distracted Driving in 2024 (DOT HS 813 790): 3,208 people killed in distraction-affected crashes in 2024
CCC Intelligent Solutions, Crash Course 2026: average third-party bodily injury paid outcome ≈ $29,100 per injured person (Q2 2025), +36% since Q4 2020
Triple-I (Insurance Information Institute), April 2026: U.S. severe convective storms (hail, tornadoes, wind) generated more than $50B in insured losses for the third consecutive year

State bans on credit-based insurance scores for auto: California (Prop 103, 1988), Hawaii, Massachusetts, Michigan (2020 reform) — Experian / NAIC summaries; industry rate studies (Bankrate, ValuePenguin 2026) find poor-credit drivers often pay roughly double for full coverage

Price optimization: prohibited or restricted by regulators in about 20 states + D.C. (Consumer Federation of America; Texas Department of Insurance 2026 bulletin); CFA letter to state commissioners, Sept 2026
J.D. Power 2026 U.S. Insurance Shopping Study: 53% of auto customers shopped, switching rate 4.5%
Telematics / usage-based insurance: insurers advertise typical savings of 10%–30% for safe drivers; in some programs risky driving can raise the price (Progressive Snapshot FAQ)
Callback: ep18 'How Insurance Companies Make Money' (the village pot)

beats.text: Dave opens his car insurance renewal. No accidents. No tickets. Not even a scratch.
Last year, he paid eighteen hundred dollars. This year? Twenty two hundred.
And he's not alone. In five years, the price of car insurance in America jumped about fifty percent. More than double regular inflation.
And here's the weird part. Some of what you pay has nothing to do with how you drive.
Your credit. Your ZIP code. Even how likely you are to shop around.
Today: the pot, the bumper, the crashes, the storms, the secret scores, the loyalty penalty, and how Dave fights back.
Let's look at Dave's letter. Same car. Same driver. Same boring commute.
Four hundred dollars more. That's a twenty two percent jump. For doing absolutely nothing wrong.
So what does a normal driver pay? According to Insurify, full coverage in America now averages about two thousand two hundred forty dollars a year.
That's about one hundred eighty seven dollars a month. Almost like a second car payment. For a car you already own.
Dave calls his insurer. The nice lady says: rates went up in your area. Dave says: but I didn't do anything! She says: I know.
The letter doesn't explain anything. Just a bigger number, and a due date.
To understand this, remember the village pot from our insurance video.
Everybody puts money in a big pot. Whoever crashes this year gets paid from the pot.
So Dave isn't really paying for his own crashes. He's paying for everybody's crashes. Everybody in his group.
When the pot gets emptied faster, everyone has to refill it. Even the careful drivers. Even Dave.
It's like splitting a restaurant bill with ten friends. You ordered a salad. But somebody ordered the lobster. Now everybody's share goes up.
And the pot got emptied fast. Government price data shows car insurance up about fifty percent in five years. Everything else? About twenty two percent.
Now, to be fair, the average dipped a little this past year. But after a fifty percent climb, a small dip doesn't feel like much.
Reason number one. Cars became computers on wheels.
An old bumper was a piece of plastic. You bump it, you replace it. A few hundred dollars.
A new bumper is full of sensors, radar, and cameras. They help the car brake by itself and park by itself. Great for safety.
But after a small crash, all of that has to be replaced and carefully aimed again. AAA found these systems can make up more than a third of the repair bill.
One front radar sensor can cost up to thirteen hundred dollars. For a part the size of a cookie.
Even the windshield. Many now have a camera behind the glass. So replacing it means new glass, plus a technician to aim the camera again.
And repair shops charge more too. Prices for car repairs are up about forty five percent in five years. So a parking lot tap can become a two thousand dollar claim.
Reason number two. When crashes happen, they cost more.
Cars got bigger and heavier. And drivers got more distracted. By what? You know what. The phone.
In twenty twenty four, the government's traffic safety agency counted more than three thousand two hundred people killed in crashes involving distracted drivers.
Then come the medical bills. And the lawyers. After a crash, more people hire lawyers, and settlements keep getting bigger.
The average payout for one injured person is now around twenty nine thousand dollars. That's up about thirty six percent since twenty twenty.
Remember the pot? Every one of those checks comes out of it. And Dave helps refill it.

beats.chapter: Hail, Storms, and Your ZIP Code
beats.text: Reason number three. The sky.
Hail the size of golf balls can dent every car in a parking lot in ten minutes. Floods can total a car in one night.
For three years in a row, severe storms in America caused more than fifty billion dollars of insured damage every year.
And that's why your ZIP code matters. Insurers look at where your car sleeps. More storms, more theft, more crashes, more lawsuits nearby? Higher price.
Two drivers. Same car. Same perfect record. But they live ten miles apart. One can pay hundreds more a year.
Dave didn't move. But his neighborhood's pot got emptied. So his price went up with it.
Now here's one most people don't know about.
In most states, insurers can use something called a credit based insurance score. It's built from your credit report.
Their data says people with lower credit scores file more claims. So they charge them more. Even with a perfect driving record.
How much more? Several rate studies find drivers with poor credit often pay around double for full coverage.
Some people call that unfair. It punishes being broke. Four states, California, Hawaii, Massachusetts and Michigan, ban it for car insurance.
Insurers say it predicts risk and keeps prices lower for most people. That's a political question. Now you know the numbers.
And now, the sneakiest one.
Most people think staying with the same insurer for years gets you the best deal. Loyalty should be rewarded, right? Often, nope.
Some insurers have used computer models to guess who won't shop around. It's called price optimization.
If the model thinks Dave is too busy or too loyal to leave, it can nudge his price up a little more each year. Not because he's riskier. Because he's comfy.
It's like a coffee shop that charges regulars more, because they know you'll come back anyway. And our old friend the raccoon approves.
About twenty states and Washington D C have banned or restricted it. And in states where regulators must approve price hikes, costs can pile up for years, then hit you all at once.
So what can Dave do? Education, not advice.
One. Shop at every renewal. Get at least three quotes. It takes about an hour, and it's the fastest way to escape the loyalty penalty.
Two. Raise your deductible, but only to an amount your emergency fund can actually pay.
Three. Bundle, and ask for every discount. Home and car together, good student, low mileage, paying yearly instead of monthly.
Four. Think about tracking apps. They can cut the price for calm drivers. But they watch how you brake, how fast you go, and when you drive. And in some programs, a bad score can cost you more.
And five. Check your credit report and fix any mistakes. In most states, it can quietly lower your price.
Dave gets four quotes. The best one is three hundred fifty dollars cheaper. Same coverage. Same funny blue car.
So let's recap.
One. You pay for everyone's crashes. When repairs, injuries and storms cost more, the whole pot gets pricier.
Two. Your price also depends on things that aren't driving. Your ZIP code, your credit, and whether you shop around.
Three. Loyalty often isn't rewarded. Compare quotes at every renewal.
Next time, Dave swears he'll finally save money. But his phone has other plans. Why can't you save money? It's not your fault. Mostly.
